newsitem.title: USA: NYC Hevesi sees $1.3 bln of one-shots in FY 1998.
newsitem.headline: NYC Hevesi sees $1.3 bln of one-shots in FY 1998.

text.p: New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi projected the city would end the 1997 fiscal year with a fat surplus but warned the mayor's proposed budget for next year posed substantial risks, a city official said Tuesday.

Hevesi estimated that the preliminary budget prepared by the Giuliani Administration for fiscal 1998 contained $1.29 bln of one-shots, according to a report that will be disclosed shortly, said the city official, who declined to be named.

The one-shots for 1998 include using part of the 1997 surplus to prepay $391 of debt, $270 million in back airport rentals, $250 million from a refunding by the Municipal Assistance Corporation for New York City, $125 million in asset sales and $200 million from the Metropolitan Transportation Agency (MTA).

Hevesi, who estimated the 1997 surplus at $220 million to $396 million, depending upon various actions the city opts to take, noted that the Giuliani Administration's preliminary budget added $208 million of one-shots to fiscal 1997. This increased the total for nonrecurring revenues for that year, which ends on June 30, to $1.44 billion.

The city comptroller, whose report is expected to soon be followed by one from the state comptroller, blasted Mayor Rudolph Giuliani's plan to give the MTA $200 million of financing next year in return of the same amount of cash.

Noting the deal's details have not been disclosed, Hevesi said the transfer appeared to involve the sale of the mid-town Coliseum. He faulted such a maneuver, saying whenever a capital asset was sold, the proceeds should be used to pay off debt or for pay-as-you-go capital.

"However, if the Coliseum is not sold, then the deal appears to be an expansion of the swap of capital for operating funds. If this is the case, the comptroller strongly opposes the transaction as a fiscal gimmick intended to provide the city with operating funds through the capital budget," Hevesi said, in his report.

The city official explained that while the fiscal 1998 budget proposed by Giuliani contained from $1.397 billion to $2.11 billion of risks, the potential gap was smaller -- $864 million to $2 billion -- because the risks were partly offset by resources, estimated at $107 million to $533 million, that were not included in the budget.
